questions.question: What does PCB stand for?
questions.explanation: The PCB (Process Control Block) is the kernel data structure that stores all state of a process: registers, PID, state, open files, memory maps, and scheduling info.

questions.question: What are the three main states of a process?
questions.explanation: Running=on CPU, Ready=waiting for CPU, Blocked=waiting for I/O or event.

questions.question: What does fork() return to the PARENT process?
questions.explanation: fork() returns the child's PID to the parent, 0 to the child, and −1 on error.

questions.question: What does fork() return to the CHILD process?
questions.explanation: fork() returns 0 to the child so it knows it is the child.

questions.question: What does exec() do when called successfully?
options: Replaces the current process image with a new program
questions.explanation: exec() replaces the calling process's code/data with a new program. It never returns on success.

questions.question: What is Limited Direct Execution (LDE)?
options: Running processes directly on CPU while OS retains control via traps
Limiting the number of direct memory accesses
Executing processes in user mode only
Running one process at a time
questions.explanation: LDE lets processes run at full speed on hardware while the OS retains control via traps and timer interrupts.

questions.question: What two CPU modes exist in LDE?
questions.explanation: User mode: limited privileges. Kernel mode: full hardware access. System calls switch between them.

questions.question: What happens when a process executes a system call?
options: CPU switches to kernel mode via a trap instruction
The OS creates a new process
Memory is allocated from the heap
questions.explanation: A trap instruction triggers a privilege switch to kernel mode, jumping to a pre-registered handler.

questions.question: What is a zombie process?
options: A process that has finished but hasn't been reaped by its parent
A process that consumes all CPU
questions.explanation: A zombie is a terminated process whose exit status hasn't been collected by the parent via wait().

questions.question: Which syscall does a parent use to wait for a child to finish?
questions.explanation: wait()/waitpid() blocks the parent until the child terminates and cleans up the zombie entry.

questions.question: Which scheduling algorithm minimizes turnaround time?
questions.explanation: STCF always runs the job closest to completion, minimizing average turnaround time.

questions.question: Which scheduling algorithm minimizes response time?
questions.explanation: RR preempts jobs on fixed time slices, giving every job quick initial response.

questions.question: What is turnaround time?
options: Time a process waits in the queue
Time from first run to completion
questions.explanation: Turnaround = T_completion − T_arrival. It measures end-to-end latency.

questions.question: What is response time?
options: First run time minus arrival time
Time to complete a system call
questions.explanation: Response time = T_firstrun − T_arrival. Measures interactivity.

questions.question: In MLFQ, where does a new job enter?
questions.explanation: New jobs enter at top priority; the scheduler demotes them over time based on behavior.

questions.question: In MLFQ, what happens when a job uses its entire time allotment?
options: It is demoted to a lower priority queue
questions.explanation: MLFQ demotes jobs that use their full allotment, assuming they are CPU-bound.

questions.question: Why does MLFQ have a periodic priority boost?
options: To prevent starvation of CPU-bound jobs
questions.explanation: Without boosts, CPU-bound jobs sink to the bottom forever. The boost resets all jobs to top priority.

questions.question: How many rules does MLFQ have?
questions.explanation: The 5 MLFQ rules cover: priority comparison, same-priority RR, new job placement, demotion on full allotment, and periodic boost.

questions.question: What data structure does Linux CFS use to store runnable processes?
questions.explanation: CFS uses a red-black tree ordered by vruntime. O(log n) insert/remove, O(1) min lookup.

questions.question: What does CFS always schedule next?
options: The process with the lowest vruntime
The process with the most tickets
questions.explanation: CFS picks the leftmost node (minimum vruntime) from the red-black tree.

questions.question: In CFS, what happens to a sleeping process's vruntime when it wakes up?
options: Set to the current minimum vruntime
Continues from where it left off
questions.explanation: Setting it to min prevents a sleeping process from getting a huge CPU burst when it wakes.

questions.question: What does a lower nice value mean in Linux?
questions.explanation: nice −20 = highest priority; nice +19 = lowest. Lower nice → higher CFS weight → slower vruntime increase.

questions.question: What is the range of nice values in Linux?
questions.explanation: Linux nice values range from −20 (highest priority) to +19 (lowest).

questions.question: What is SQMS?
options: Single-Queue Multiprocessor Scheduling — one global queue for all CPUs
questions.explanation: SQMS is the simplest multiprocessor scheduler: one queue, all CPUs dequeue from it.

questions.question: What is the main problem with SQMS?
options: Lock contention and poor cache affinity
questions.explanation: Every CPU must lock the queue to dequeue, causing contention. No affinity means cold cache on every reschedule.

questions.question: What is cache affinity in scheduling?
options: Preferring to run a process on the same CPU it last ran on
The tendency of caches to fill up
Matching cache size to process size
Keeping related processes on the same CPU
questions.explanation: A process builds warm cache state on a CPU. Rescheduling it to another CPU causes cache misses.

questions.question: In MQMS, how is load balancing achieved?
options: Work stealing — idle CPUs steal jobs from busy queues
questions.explanation: An idle CPU peeks at another CPU's queue and steals jobs. Frequency is a tunable trade-off.

questions.question: Is SJF preemptive or non-preemptive?
questions.explanation: SJF runs the shortest job to completion without preemption. STCF is its preemptive variant.

questions.question: How does MLFQ prevent gaming via repeated I/O?
options: Count total CPU time used at a level, not just per-slice
Only allow I/O from low-priority queues
Limit I/O calls per time slice
questions.explanation: Counting total time prevents a process from resetting its counter by issuing I/O just before the slice expires.

questions.question: What scheduling algorithm does MLFQ approximate?
questions.explanation: MLFQ approximates STCF by using past behavior to infer job length, without needing it upfront.

questions.question: Is the address printed by printf("%p", ptr) virtual or physical?
questions.explanation: User-space code always sees virtual addresses. Physical addresses are hidden by the MMU.

questions.question: What does MMU stand for?
questions.explanation: The MMU is a hardware unit inside the CPU that translates VA→PA on every memory access.

questions.question: In the base+bounds scheme, how is the physical address calculated?
questions.explanation: Simple addition: the base register shifts the virtual address to its physical location. Bounds catches violations.

questions.question: What is external fragmentation?
options: Free memory in non-contiguous chunks too small for a large request
Wasted space inside an allocated chunk
Memory lost when a process exits
Space wasted by the page table
questions.explanation: External fragmentation is the classic problem with variable-size allocation: many small holes, no big contiguous block.

questions.question: What is internal fragmentation?
options: Wasted space inside an allocated chunk
questions.explanation: If you request 9 bytes and get 16, 7 bytes are wasted inside your allocation — that's internal fragmentation.

questions.question: What is coalescing in memory management?
options: Merging adjacent free chunks into one larger chunk
questions.explanation: Coalescing runs on free() to merge neighboring free blocks, preventing the free list from fragmenting.

questions.question: Which syscall expands the heap?
questions.explanation: sbrk()/brk() move the program break (end of heap) upward. malloc() calls sbrk() when it needs more space.

questions.question: What is segmentation?
options: Dividing the address space into logical segments each with base+bounds
questions.explanation: Segmentation gives each segment (code, heap, stack) its own base+bounds pair, allowing independent placement.

questions.question: What is the main problem with segmentation?
questions.explanation: As segments are allocated and freed, physical memory becomes riddled with small unusable gaps.

questions.question: Can two processes share the same virtual address?
options: Yes — each has its own independent virtual address space
No — virtual addresses must be unique system-wide
questions.explanation: Each process has a private virtual address space. Two processes can both have pointer 0x1000 — they map to different physical locations.

questions.question: In which direction does the heap grow?
questions.explanation: Heap grows up; stack grows down. They grow toward each other.

questions.question: In which direction does the stack grow?
questions.explanation: On x86 and most architectures, the stack grows toward lower addresses (toward the heap).

questions.question: What is a free list?
options: A linked list of free memory chunks used by the allocator
A list of processes with no owner
A list of available CPU cores
A list of free file descriptors
questions.explanation: The allocator maintains a free list to track available chunks. malloc() searches it; free() inserts into it.

questions.question: What is interposing in hardware-software systems?
options: Inserting a transparent layer between a requester and a resource
questions.explanation: The MMU interposes on every memory access: user code requests virtual address V, but physically accesses P — transparently.

questions.question: What is the best-fit allocation strategy?
options: Find the smallest chunk that satisfies the request
Use the first chunk that fits
Start search from the last allocation
questions.explanation: Best-fit minimizes internal waste but can create many tiny leftover fragments causing external fragmentation.

questions.question: What is the typical page size on modern systems?
questions.explanation: 4KB (4096 bytes) is the default page size on x86 and most modern architectures.

questions.question: In a 32-bit address space with 4KB pages, how many page table entries are needed?
questions.explanation: 32-bit VA space / 12-bit offset = 20-bit VPN → 2^20 = ~1M entries per process.

questions.question: In a 32-bit address space with 4KB pages and 4-byte PTEs, how large is one page table?
questions.explanation: 2^20 entries × 4 bytes/entry = 4 MB per process. With many processes, this is significant.

questions.question: With 4KB pages, how many offset bits are in a virtual address?
questions.explanation: Offset bits = log2(page size) = log2(4096) = 12 bits.

questions.question: With a 32-bit VA and 4KB pages, how many VPN bits are there?
questions.explanation: VPN bits = VA bits − offset bits = 32 − 12 = 20 bits.

questions.question: What is a TLB?
options: A hardware cache of VA→PA translations inside the MMU
A software table listing memory allocations
A translation buffer in the OS kernel
questions.explanation: The TLB caches recent page table lookups so the CPU doesn't access memory for every translation.

questions.question: What happens on a TLB hit?
options: Hardware reads PFN directly — no memory access needed
OS is invoked to handle translation
Page table is read from memory
questions.explanation: TLB hit = fast path: hardware finds VPN in cache, reads PFN instantly. Very common due to locality.

questions.question: On x86, what handles a TLB miss?
options: Hardware — walks the page table automatically
questions.explanation: x86 has a hardware page-table walker. On TLB miss, hardware walks CR3→PD→PT and loads the entry.

questions.question: On MIPS/RISC-V, what handles a TLB miss?
questions.explanation: Software-managed TLBs raise a TLB-miss trap. The OS handler looks up the page table and loads the entry.

questions.question: What is an ASID?
options: Address Space ID — tags TLB entries per process to avoid full flush on context switch
questions.explanation: ASID tags each TLB entry with a process identifier. On context switch, entries from other processes are ignored.

questions.question: What does the Present bit in a PTE mean?
options: Page is in physical memory (0 = on disk → page fault)
questions.explanation: Present=0 means the page was swapped out. The PTE then stores the swap offset instead of PFN.

questions.question: What does the Dirty bit in a PTE mean?
options: Page has been written and must be flushed to disk before eviction
questions.explanation: The dirty bit is set by hardware on any write. A dirty page must be written to disk before eviction.

questions.question: What does CR3 hold on x86?
options: Physical address of the page table root
questions.explanation: CR3 points to the top-level page directory. The OS updates CR3 on every context switch.

questions.question: What does the Valid bit in a TLB entry mean?
options: This TLB entry holds a usable mapping
The page is in physical memory
The VPN exists in the page table
questions.explanation: Valid=0 means the TLB slot is unused. After a flush, all entries are marked invalid.

questions.question: What is the difference between the Present bit and the Valid bit?
options: Present (PTE): page in RAM; Valid (TLB): entry is usable
Valid (PTE): legal mapping; Present (TLB): page in RAM
Both indicate the page is in RAM
questions.explanation: Present is a PTE concept (is the page in RAM?). Valid is a TLB concept (does this slot hold a real mapping?).

questions.question: What problem do multi-level page tables solve?
options: Memory waste from large page tables in sparse address spaces
questions.explanation: Only allocate PT pages for virtual memory actually in use. Sparse address spaces → very small page tables.

questions.question: What is the cost of multi-level page tables vs. single-level?
options: TLB miss requires 2–4 memory accesses instead of 1
questions.explanation: Each level of the page table requires a separate memory access on a TLB miss.

questions.question: Why is paging slow without hardware support?
options: Every memory access requires 2 accesses: page table lookup + actual data
Page tables are stored on disk
Pages must be locked during access
The OS must handle every translation
questions.explanation: Without a TLB, every load/store requires one extra memory access to look up the page table.

questions.question: What is a huge page (superpage)?
options: A larger page (2MB or 1GB) that covers more memory with fewer TLB entries
A page shared between many processes
A page that spans multiple physical frames
A page with extra protection bits
questions.explanation: Huge pages reduce TLB pressure for large working sets, at the cost of potential internal fragmentation.

questions.question: What is the fully-associative TLB structure?
options: Any VPN can be stored in any TLB slot; all slots searched in parallel
VPN maps to a fixed TLB slot
Only recent VPNs can be stored
questions.explanation: Fully associative = any VPN can go anywhere; hardware checks all entries simultaneously.

questions.question: What is swap space?
options: Reserved disk area for pages that don't fit in physical memory
A buffer between CPU and RAM
Space reserved for the page table
questions.explanation: Swap lets the OS support address spaces larger than physical RAM by storing cold pages on disk.

questions.question: What happens during a page fault?
options: OS loads the missing page from disk, updates PTE, retries the instruction
A new page is allocated from heap
questions.explanation: Page fault handler: find swap offset in PTE → read page from disk → put in free frame → update PTE → retry.

questions.question: When does the OS proactively start evicting pages?
options: When free frames fall below the low watermark
questions.explanation: The high/low watermark mechanism starts kswapd early, before memory is exhausted.

questions.question: What is the name of the Linux background page eviction daemon?
questions.explanation: kswapd runs in the background, proactively freeing pages to maintain the low-watermark.

questions.question: What is thrashing?
options: Spending more time swapping pages than doing useful work
questions.explanation: Thrashing: OS evicts a page, then immediately needs it again. Working set > physical memory.

questions.question: In the Clock algorithm, what happens when reference bit = 1?
options: Bit is cleared, page gets a second chance
questions.explanation: The clock hand gives the page a second chance by clearing the bit, then moves on.

questions.question: In the Clock algorithm, what happens when reference bit = 0?
questions.explanation: Reference bit = 0 means the page hasn't been accessed since the last sweep → evict it.

questions.question: Why is evicting a dirty page more expensive than a clean page?
options: Dirty page must be written to disk first; clean page can just be discarded
questions.explanation: A clean page is already on disk (unchanged). A dirty page must be written back before the frame can be reused.

questions.question: What is Copy-On-Write (COW)?
options: Parent and child share frames read-only; private copy made only on first write
OS copies all pages on fork() immediately
Files are copied when opened for writing
Cache lines copied on cache miss
questions.explanation: COW defers copying until actually needed. fork() + exec() becomes nearly free since child just overwrites.

questions.question: COW is primarily used during which syscall?
questions.explanation: fork() uses COW to avoid immediately copying all parent pages. Only modified pages get private copies.

questions.question: What is the LRU replacement policy?
options: Evict the page not used for the longest time
Evict the page with the smallest page number
Evict the page with the lowest reference count
questions.explanation: LRU is optimal in practice but expensive to implement exactly. Clock algorithm approximates it.

questions.question: If a PTE's present bit = 0, what does the rest of the PTE store?
options: The disk address (swap offset) where the page can be found
The PFN of a different page
questions.explanation: When a page is swapped out, the OS puts its swap offset in the PTE so it can be retrieved on a page fault.

questions.question: What is the OOM killer?
options: Linux mechanism that terminates processes when memory is exhausted
questions.explanation: When all memory + swap is consumed, the OOM killer selects a process to terminate to free memory.

questions.question: What is the working set of a process?
options: The set of pages actively used by a process at a given time
questions.explanation: If the working set fits in physical memory, no thrashing. If not, the system thrashes.

questions.question: Which page replacement policy is theoretically optimal?
options: OPT / Belady's algorithm — evict the page used farthest in the future
questions.explanation: OPT requires future knowledge (impossible in practice) but serves as a benchmark for real policies.

questions.question: Why does null pointer dereference cause a segfault?
options: Address 0 is unmapped; MMU raises protection fault → SIGSEGV
The compiler inserts a null check
questions.explanation: Linux intentionally leaves the first page (0–4KB) unmapped. Any access causes a protection fault.

questions.question: In Linux 64-bit, where is kernel space?
options: At the high end of the virtual address space
questions.explanation: Kernel space occupies the upper portion (0xFFFF800000000000+). User space is below 0x00007FFFFFFFFFFF.

questions.question: Why is the kernel mapped into every process's address space?
options: To avoid TLB flushes on system calls
So processes can call kernel directly
questions.explanation: Keeping kernel mapped means syscall entry/return doesn't flush the TLB — a significant performance win.

questions.question: What happens to the TLB on context switch without ASIDs?
questions.explanation: Without ASIDs, all TLB entries are from the previous process and must be invalidated.

questions.question: What scheduling class handles normal user processes in Linux?
questions.explanation: SCHED_NORMAL uses CFS. SCHED_RT is for real-time processes with strict latency requirements.

questions.question: What is the BSS segment?
options: Uninitialized global/static data, zeroed at program start
questions.explanation: BSS (Block Started by Symbol) holds uninitialized globals/statics. The OS zeros it at load time.

questions.question: What does mmap(MAP_SHARED) do?
options: Maps a file into memory shared between processes — writes visible to all
Maps the stack into a file
questions.explanation: MAP_SHARED: writes to the mapped region go directly to the underlying file and are visible to other mappers.

questions.question: What does mmap(MAP_PRIVATE) do?
options: Creates a COW mapping — writes create private copies
Maps a file shared between processes
Maps the heap to a file
questions.explanation: MAP_PRIVATE uses COW: initially shares the file/pages, but writes create process-private copies.

questions.question: What is bus snooping?
options: Caches monitor the memory bus to maintain coherent views across CPUs
A technique for detecting bus errors
questions.explanation: With bus snooping, when CPU A writes to an address cached by CPU B, CPU B's cache is automatically invalidated.

questions.question: What are the two types of cache locality?
options: Temporal (same address again soon) and Spatial (nearby addresses soon)
questions.explanation: Temporal: recently used data will be used again. Spatial: data near used addresses will be used. Both justify caching.

questions.question: A 16-bit VA space with 512-byte pages. How many offset bits?
questions.explanation: Offset bits = log2(512) = 9.

questions.question: 16-bit VA, 512-byte pages. How many VPN bits?
questions.explanation: VPN bits = 16 − 9 = 7.

questions.question: 16-bit VA, 512-byte pages. How many page table entries?
questions.explanation: 2^7 = 128 entries. With 4 bytes each → page table is 512 bytes.

questions.question: 32-bit VA, 8KB pages. How many offset bits?
32-bit VA, 8KB pages. How many VPN bits?
questions.explanation: 32 − 13 = 19 VPN bits → 2^19 = 524,288 entries per process.

questions.question: 32-bit VA, 8KB pages, 4-byte PTEs. How large is the page table?
Virtual address 0x0001F3AC, 4KB pages (12-bit offset). What is the offset?
questions.explanation: Low 12 bits of 0x0001F3AC = 0x3AC = 940 decimal.

questions.question: Virtual address 0x0001F3AC, 4KB pages. What is the VPN?
PFN = 5, page size = 4096. What is the base physical address of this frame?
questions.explanation: Physical base = PFN × page_size = 5 × 4096 = 20480.

questions.question: With a 2-level page table (10-bit PD index | 10-bit PT index | 12-bit offset): PD[2][3] -> PFN=9. VA has PD=2, PT=3, offset=0x10. Physical address?
questions.explanation: Physical = PFN x page_size + offset = 9 x 4096 + 16 = 36864 + 16 = 36880.

questions.question: What problem does the Singleton pattern solve?
options: Ensuring a class has only one instance with global access
Providing an interface for creating families of objects
Separating object construction from its representation
Defining a skeleton algorithm in a base class
questions.explanation: Singleton ensures exactly one instance exists and provides a global access point. Classic use: logging system, config manager, connection pool.

questions.question: Which Singleton implementation is thread-safe in C++11 without explicit locking?
options: Using a global variable with extern
questions.explanation: C++11 guarantees function-local statics are initialized exactly once even under concurrent calls. `static Logger& get() { static Logger inst; return inst; }` is the idiomatic Meyers Singleton.

questions.question: What is the main drawback of the Singleton pattern?
options: It introduces global state, making unit testing hard
It allocates on the heap by default
questions.explanation: Global state hidden behind a class interface makes dependencies implicit, hinders testability, and creates tight coupling. Prefer dependency injection when possible.

questions.question: In Python, what is the simplest way to implement a Singleton?
options: Using a module — a module is imported once and acts as a singleton
questions.explanation: In Python, a module is loaded once per interpreter session. Placing singleton state at module level is idiomatic. Metaclass or __new__ approaches work but are more verbose.

questions.question: What distinguishes Factory Method from Abstract Factory?
options: Factory Method creates one product via a single method; Abstract Factory creates families of related products
Abstract Factory uses inheritance; Factory Method uses composition
Factory Method is for runtime creation; Abstract Factory is for compile time
They are identical patterns with different names
questions.explanation: Factory Method defines one factory method subclasses override to create a product. Abstract Factory groups multiple factory methods to produce a family of compatible objects (e.g., UI widgets for a given OS theme).

questions.question: In a trading system, which creational pattern best handles creating different order types (Market, Limit, Stop)?
options: Factory Method — a base OrderFactory subclassed per order type
Singleton — one factory for all orders
questions.explanation: Factory Method lets you define a createOrder() interface in a base class and override it per concrete factory (MarketOrderFactory, LimitOrderFactory), keeping client code decoupled from concrete types.

questions.question: What does the Builder pattern separate?
options: The construction of a complex object from its representation
The algorithm from the data structure
questions.explanation: Builder separates 'how to build' from 'what you get'. A Director drives the construction steps; a ConcreteBuilder assembles parts; the client gets the finished product. Useful for FIX message construction.

questions.question: Which Python idiom resembles the Builder pattern natively?
options: Method chaining with keyword arguments and a build() method
questions.explanation: Python builders often chain setter calls: `Order().symbol('AAPL').qty(100).side('BUY').build()`. The `@dataclass` with `field(default_factory=...)` covers simpler cases but doesn't model multi-step construction.

questions.question: When is the Prototype pattern preferred over Factory?
options: When object creation is expensive and cloning a cached instance is faster
When you need exactly one instance
When you need multiple product families
When construction has many optional parameters
questions.explanation: Prototype is ideal when instantiation is costly (e.g., deep copying a pre-built risk model or instrument universe) and you can clone a known-good object rather than rebuild from scratch.

questions.question: In C++, deep vs shallow copy is critical for Prototype. What does `std::vector` provide by default?
options: Deep copy — the copy constructor copies all elements
Shallow copy — only the pointer is copied
questions.explanation: `std::vector`'s copy constructor allocates new storage and copies every element. A shallow copy would share the buffer, causing double-free bugs. Understanding this is critical when implementing Prototype in C++.

questions.question: Abstract Factory is useful in quant systems for:
options: Creating compatible sets of market data feeds, order routers, and risk engines per venue
Ensuring only one risk engine exists
Building FIX messages step by step
questions.explanation: An Abstract Factory can produce a family of venue-compatible components: `VenueFactory::createFeed()`, `createRouter()`, `createRiskEngine()`. Swapping from CME to LSE factory swaps the entire stack consistently.

questions.question: What is the 'virtual constructor' idiom in C++?
options: A virtual clone() method that calls the copy constructor — effectively Prototype
questions.explanation: C++ constructors cannot be virtual, but you can simulate it with a virtual `clone()` method. This is the C++ idiom for Prototype: `virtual Base* clone() const { return new Derived(*this); }`.

questions.question: Which statement about the Builder pattern in C++ is TRUE?
options: Named parameter idiom via method chaining achieves Builder without a separate Director
Builder always requires a Director class
Builder and Factory Method are interchangeable
questions.explanation: The named parameter idiom `Widget w = WidgetBuilder().width(100).height(200).title("Chart").build()` is an idiomatic C++ Builder. A Director is optional — the client can call steps directly.

questions.question: A Singleton OrderManager in a multi-threaded trading system MUST:
options: Ensure thread-safe lazy initialization and protect shared state with mutexes or atomics
Always be eagerly initialized at program start
Use a global variable for fastest access
Avoid any locking to minimize latency
questions.explanation: Thread safety is non-negotiable. Either use Meyers singleton (C++11 static local), `std::call_once`, or double-checked locking with `std::atomic`. Unprotected lazy init under threads leads to data races.

questions.question: In Python, how does `__new__` differ from `__init__` in context of Singleton?
options: __new__ creates the instance; __init__ initializes it — Singleton intercepts __new__ to return the same instance
questions.explanation: `__new__` is the actual constructor (allocates and returns the instance). A Singleton metaclass overrides `__new__` or `__call__` to return the cached instance rather than creating a new one.

questions.question: Which C++ feature makes Abstract Factory safer with modern C++?
options: std::unique_ptr return types eliminate ownership ambiguity
Virtual destructors are unnecessary with smart pointers
questions.explanation: Returning `std::unique_ptr<Product>` from factory methods makes ownership transfer explicit and prevents leaks. `std::make_unique<ConcreteProduct>()` is the idiomatic factory return in modern C++.

questions.question: What is the Object Pool pattern and when is it relevant in quant systems?
options: Pre-allocating a pool of reusable objects to avoid dynamic allocation in hot paths
A way to lazily create objects on demand
questions.explanation: Object Pool pre-creates a fixed set of reusable objects (e.g., order objects, FIX messages) to eliminate heap allocation in latency-sensitive hot paths. Critical in HFT where `new`/`delete` costs microseconds.

questions.question: Which pattern creates objects by copying a prototypical instance, and is closest to Python's `copy.deepcopy()`?
questions.explanation: Prototype pattern directly maps to Python's `copy.deepcopy()`. The idea: instead of re-constructing, clone an existing configured object. Useful for cloning pre-configured strategy objects.

questions.question: What is a key difference between Factory Method and simply using a constructor?
options: Factory Method decouples the client from concrete types via a virtual method; constructors are always concrete
Factory Method eliminates the need for inheritance
questions.explanation: A constructor binds the caller to a specific type. Factory Method returns a base-class pointer/reference to a concrete subtype decided at runtime, enabling substitution and polymorphism without changing client code.

questions.question: In Python, what does `@classmethod` enable that supports the Factory pattern?
questions.explanation: `@classmethod` methods are the idiomatic Python Factory — they return `cls(...)` instances with descriptive names. `datetime.fromtimestamp()`, `dict.fromkeys()` are stdlib examples.

questions.question: The Builder pattern helps most when:
options: A class has many optional parameters and combinations, like a complex FIX order with 20+ fields
You want to share a single object among many clients
You need to iterate over a collection
questions.explanation: Without Builder, a constructor with 20 parameters forces callers to remember order and meaning. Builder makes each parameter explicit: `order.price(100.5).qty(500).timeInForce(IOC)`.

questions.question: What is 'telescoping constructor' anti-pattern and which creational pattern solves it?
options: Many overloaded constructors with increasing parameters — Builder solves it
Using too many Singletons — Factory solves it
Creating objects too eagerly — Prototype solves it
Overusing inheritance — Abstract Factory solves it
questions.explanation: Telescoping constructors: `Order(sym)`, `Order(sym,qty)`, `Order(sym,qty,price)`, ... become unmanageable. Builder replaces this with a fluent interface where only required fields are mandatory.

questions.question: A C++ `std::make_shared<T>()` is closest in intent to which pattern?
options: Factory Method — it encapsulates object creation behind a function call
Builder — it constructs step by step
Prototype — it clones an existing object
questions.explanation: `std::make_shared` is a factory function: it allocates and constructs in one call, returning a `shared_ptr`. This is the Factory Method pattern applied to smart pointer creation — decoupling allocation from usage.

questions.question: When implementing a Singleton configuration reader in Python, which approach has the LEAST hidden state?
options: Dependency injection — pass the config object explicitly rather than using a Singleton
questions.explanation: All Singleton approaches introduce global state. Dependency injection (passing config as a constructor argument) is more testable and explicit. Use Singleton only when the global nature is genuinely intentional.

questions.question: Abstract Factory vs Dependency Injection: which statement is TRUE?
options: DI frameworks often use Abstract Factory internally to create dependencies
Abstract Factory requires a DI container
DI eliminates the need for factories entirely
questions.explanation: Modern DI containers (Spring, Guice, Python's dependency-injector) use factory functions or provider classes — essentially Abstract Factories — to create and wire dependencies. The patterns complement each other.

questions.question: What is the intent of the Adapter pattern?
options: Convert an interface into another interface clients expect — make incompatible interfaces work together
Add responsibilities to an object dynamically
Provide a simplified interface to a complex subsystem
Share a fine-grained object to support large numbers efficiently
questions.explanation: Adapter wraps an existing class to make it compatible with a required interface. Example: wrapping a legacy FIX 4.2 order handler to expose a modern order interface without modifying the legacy code.

questions.question: In C++, which two Adapter implementations exist?
options: Class adapter (multiple inheritance) and object adapter (composition)
questions.explanation: Class adapter inherits from both the target interface and the adaptee (multiple inheritance). Object adapter holds a pointer to the adaptee and implements the target interface via composition. Object adapter is preferred.

questions.question: A Python `@property` wrapping a private attribute exemplifies which structural pattern?
options: Proxy — it controls access to the underlying attribute
questions.explanation: A `@property` is a Proxy: it intercepts attribute access, potentially adding validation, lazy loading, or logging, without changing the external interface. The underlying `_value` is the real subject.

questions.question: What distinguishes Decorator from inheritance for adding behavior?
options: Decorator composes behavior at runtime; inheritance is compile-time and creates class explosion
Inheritance is preferred for adding behavior
questions.explanation: Inheritance requires a new class per combination. If you have 3 order types and 4 validations, inheritance needs 12 classes. Decorator stacks wraps: `LoggingOrder(RiskCheckedOrder(MarketOrder()))`.

questions.question: In Python, what is the idiomatic Decorator pattern?
options: Function decorators with @functools.wraps preserving metadata, or classes implementing __call__
questions.explanation: `@timer`, `@retry`, `@cache` are Python decorators implementing the pattern. `@functools.wraps` preserves `__name__` and `__doc__`. Class decorators implement `__call__` and delegate to the wrapped object.

questions.question: The Facade pattern is used when:
options: You want to provide a simple interface to a complex subsystem of classes
You need to adapt one interface to another
You want to add behavior without subclassing
You want to share fine-grained state
questions.explanation: Facade hides complexity. A TradingFacade might expose `place_order(sym, qty)` while internally coordinating RiskEngine, OrderRouter, MarketDataFeed, and AuditLogger — callers need not know any of that.

questions.question: How does Facade differ from Adapter?
options: Facade simplifies an existing interface; Adapter makes two incompatible interfaces work together
Facade requires inheritance; Adapter uses composition
questions.explanation: Adapter is about interface compatibility (making A look like B). Facade is about convenience (hiding N complex classes behind one simple one). Facade doesn't need to match any pre-existing interface.

questions.question: The Flyweight pattern reduces memory by:
options: Sharing intrinsic (immutable) state among many objects, storing extrinsic state externally
questions.explanation: Flyweight splits object state into intrinsic (shared, e.g., instrument symbol, tick size) and extrinsic (per-use, e.g., position size). A shared Instrument object is reused across thousands of positions.

questions.question: In a trading system with 1M+ positions, how does Flyweight apply?
options: Store instrument metadata (symbol, exchange, tick size) once in a shared Flyweight; each Position holds only a reference plus its unique quantity/price
Each position stores a full copy of instrument data
Instrument data is recalculated on demand
questions.explanation: If each of 1M positions held a full copy of instrument data (200 bytes), you'd need 200MB just for metadata. Flyweight stores it once per instrument and all positions share a pointer — saving orders of magnitude.

questions.question: What is the Proxy pattern's primary use?
options: Control access to another object — can add lazy init, access control, logging, or caching
questions.explanation: Proxy types: Virtual (lazy init), Protection (access control), Remote (network transparency), Logging/Caching (cross-cutting concerns). Python's `__getattr__` makes transparent proxies easy to implement.

questions.question: Which C++ standard library class exemplifies the Proxy pattern?
options: std::vector<bool> — its operator[] returns a proxy object, not a real bool reference
questions.explanation: `std::vector<bool>` is notorious: bit-packing means `v[i]` returns a `__bit_reference` proxy, not `bool&`. This breaks generic code expecting references — a famous footgun from Proxy overuse.

questions.question: In Python, `__getattr__` and `__setattr__` are typically used to implement:
options: A transparent Proxy or Decorator that forwards attribute access to a wrapped object
questions.explanation: A transparent proxy class overrides `__getattr__` to forward unknown attributes to `self._wrapped`. This allows adding logging, access control, or lazy loading without modifying the wrapped object.

questions.question: Bridge pattern separates:
options: Abstraction from implementation so they can vary independently
questions.explanation: Bridge avoids a Cartesian product of classes. Without it: if you have 3 shapes × 3 renderers = 9 classes. With Bridge: Shape holds a Renderer reference — 3 + 3 = 6 classes, varying independently.

questions.question: Composite pattern is used to:
options: Treat individual objects and compositions of objects uniformly through a common interface
questions.explanation: Composite builds tree structures. An OrderBasket containing individual orders and sub-baskets all implement the same IOrder interface — callers treat a basket of 100 orders identically to a single order.

questions.question: A smart pointer like `std::shared_ptr` in C++ implements which pattern?
options: Proxy — it controls access to the underlying object and manages its lifetime
questions.explanation: `shared_ptr` is a reference-counting Proxy: it intercepts destruction (via custom deleter), tracks owners, and can add custom access logic. Dereferencing it transparently accesses the real object.

questions.question: When should you NOT use Decorator?
options: When the wrapped interface has many methods — you must forward all of them, causing boilerplate
When you want runtime behavior composition
When subclassing would cause a class explosion
questions.explanation: If an interface has 30 methods and you decorate 10 of them, you must still implement (forward) the other 20. This boilerplate is a cost of Decorator vs. inheritance. In Python, `__getattr__` mitigates this.

questions.question: In C++, the Adapter pattern via templates (policy-based design) is called:
options: Static polymorphism / policy-based design — adapting behavior at compile time via template parameters
questions.explanation: Template Adapter: `template<class Socket> class OrderRouter { Socket s; }` where Socket can be TcpSocket or UdpSocket. The 'adaptation' is compile-time, zero-overhead — no virtual dispatch needed.

questions.question: Facade vs. Mediator: what is the key difference?
options: Facade provides a simplified interface to a subsystem (one-directional); Mediator coordinates communication between objects (bi-directional)
Facade uses inheritance; Mediator uses composition
questions.explanation: Facade: unidirectional simplification — client talks to Facade, Facade talks to subsystem. Mediator: central hub coordinating peer communication — objects don't talk to each other, only to the Mediator.

questions.question: In Python, `functools.lru_cache` implements which structural pattern?
options: Proxy with caching — it intercepts function calls and returns cached results
Adapter — it changes the function interface
questions.explanation: `lru_cache` wraps a function (Proxy semantics) and adds caching behavior. The original function is unchanged; the proxy intercepts calls, checks the cache, and only delegates on misses. Syntactically a Python decorator.

questions.question: Which pattern is most appropriate for implementing lazy loading of a heavy market data object?
options: Virtual Proxy — returns a lightweight proxy that loads the real object only on first access
questions.explanation: Virtual Proxy: `MarketDataProxy` returns a stub. On first method call, it loads the real `MarketData` object and delegates. Subsequent calls go directly. This defers expensive I/O until actually needed.

questions.question: What is 'object slicing' in C++ and which structural pattern can prevent it?
options: Assigning a derived object to a base by value truncates derived data — Proxy (via pointer) prevents it
questions.explanation: Slicing: `Base b = derived;` loses the derived part. Using a Proxy or smart pointer (`unique_ptr<Base>` pointing to a Derived) preserves polymorphism. Always pass by pointer/reference for structural patterns.

questions.question: In a quant system, wrapping a third-party market data API to match your internal `IFeed` interface uses which pattern?
questions.explanation: Adapter: the third-party API has incompatible methods (`getQuote(ticker)` vs your `subscribe(Symbol, Callback)`). An Adapter wraps it and maps calls, without modifying the third-party library.

questions.question: Composite pattern + Iterator: why are they often paired?
options: Composite builds hierarchical structures; Iterator provides a uniform way to traverse them without exposing internal structure
Iterator replaces Composite for tree traversal
questions.explanation: A portfolio tree (Composite) benefits from an Iterator that traverses all leaf positions depth-first. The client calls `for position in portfolio:` without knowing whether it's a leaf, basket, or sub-portfolio.

questions.question: In Python, which built-in feature is a Flyweight?
options: String interning — Python caches small strings and integers, returning the same object for equal values
questions.explanation: Python interns small integers (-5 to 256) and short strings. `a = 100; b = 100; a is b` is `True` — same object. This is Flyweight: a shared pool of immutable objects. `sys.intern()` extends this.

questions.question: What does SOLID's Liskov Substitution Principle require of structural patterns?
options: Any proxy, adapter, or decorator must be substitutable for the wrapped type — it must honor the base contract
You must use composition over inheritance
Every class must have a single responsibility
questions.explanation: LSP: a Proxy wrapping `IOrderRouter` must behave as an `IOrderRouter`. If the proxy throws extra exceptions or changes semantics, LSP is violated. Good structural patterns are transparent to clients.

questions.question: What is the Observer pattern?
options: Define a one-to-many dependency so that when one object changes state, all dependents are notified automatically
Encapsulate a request as an object
Define the skeleton of an algorithm, deferring steps to subclasses
Allow an object to alter its behavior when its internal state changes
questions.explanation: Observer (Publish-Subscribe): a Subject maintains a list of Observers and notifies them on state change. In trading: a price feed (Subject) notifying all subscribed strategies (Observers) on tick updates.

questions.question: In Python, which built-in mechanism natively implements Observer?
options: Callbacks/event listeners, or libraries like `blinker` and `PyDispatcher`; asyncio events for async observers
questions.explanation: Python has no built-in Observer, but callbacks (list of functions) are the simplest implementation. `signal.connect(handler)` (blinker) or asyncio `Event` for async. GUI frameworks (Qt, tkinter) use it heavily.

questions.question: What problem does the Strategy pattern solve?
options: Define a family of algorithms, encapsulate each one, and make them interchangeable at runtime
Ensure only one instance of a class
questions.explanation: Strategy replaces large if-else chains for algorithm selection. A backtester can swap `ExecutionStrategy` (VWAP, TWAP, POV) without changing the backtesting engine — just inject a different strategy object.

questions.question: In Python, functions are first-class objects. How does this simplify Strategy?
options: Pass a function directly as the strategy — no interface class needed
You still need an abstract base class
questions.explanation: Python Strategy: `def twap(order): ...` then `backtester.execute(order, strategy=twap)`. No abstract class needed. `strategy` is just a callable. This is idiomatic Python — use typing.Protocol or ABC only when needed.

questions.question: Command pattern encapsulates:
options: A request as an object, enabling undo/redo, queuing, and logging of operations
questions.explanation: Command wraps `execute()` + optionally `undo()` in an object. An OrderCommand(`BUY AAPL 100`) can be queued, logged, retried, and undone. Essential for order management systems with audit trails.

questions.question: Which C++ standard library feature directly implements the Command pattern?
options: std::function and std::bind — encapsulate callable objects for deferred execution
questions.explanation: `std::function<void()>` stores any callable (lambda, functor, bound member). This is Command: store the operation, pass it around, execute later. `std::queue<std::function<void()>>` is a command queue.

questions.question: Iterator pattern provides:
options: Sequential access to elements of a collection without exposing its underlying representation
A simplified interface to a subsystem
questions.explanation: Iterator decouples traversal from collection structure. Whether iterating a list, tree, or database cursor, client code is the same: `for item in collection`. C++ range-for and Python `__iter__`/`__next__` implement this.

questions.question: In C++, what makes a type iterable in a range-for loop?
options: It must provide begin() and end() returning iterators with operator++, operator*, and operator!=
It must be a STL container
It must have a size() method
questions.explanation: The range-for `for (auto x : coll)` calls `begin(coll)` and `end(coll)` (ADL). The returned iterators need `operator++` (advance), `operator*` (dereference), and `operator!=` (termination check).

questions.question: Python generators (`yield`) implement which pattern?
options: Iterator — they produce values lazily one at a time via __next__
Observer — they push values to subscribers
questions.explanation: A generator function returns a generator object implementing `__iter__` and `__next__`. It is an Iterator that produces values lazily. `yield` suspends and resumes execution, perfect for streaming market data.

questions.question: The Mediator pattern reduces coupling by:
options: Centralizing communication — objects don't refer to each other directly, only to the mediator
questions.explanation: Without Mediator: N objects with O(N^2) connections. With Mediator: N objects each connected only to the Mediator — O(N). An order management system mediator coordinates risk, routing, and position components.

questions.question: State pattern vs. Strategy: what is the key distinction?
options: State's algorithm changes based on internal state transitions (the object knows its state); Strategy is injected externally
Strategy changes state; State chooses strategy
State uses inheritance; Strategy uses composition
questions.explanation: State: an Order object transitions through NEW→PENDING→FILLED states, with behavior changing per state. The state object may trigger transitions. Strategy: the algorithm is injected from outside, no state transitions.

questions.question: Template Method pattern defines:
options: A skeleton algorithm in a base class with steps deferred to subclasses via virtual methods
questions.explanation: Template Method: `void Backtester::run() { loadData(); for(bar: data) { signal=generateSignal(bar); execute(signal); }; report(); }` — the skeleton is fixed, `generateSignal` is virtual and overridden per strategy.

questions.question: In Python, Template Method is often replaced by:
options: Passing hook functions as parameters (Strategy) or using abstract base classes with @abstractmethod
questions.explanation: Python's duck typing means you can pass callables as hooks rather than subclassing. But ABCs with `@abstractmethod` provide the Template Method structure explicitly when you want enforced overriding.

questions.question: What is the Null Object pattern?
options: An object implementing an interface with do-nothing behavior, eliminating null checks in client code
A pattern for creating null pointers safely
A way to handle NoneType errors
questions.explanation: Instead of `if logger: logger.log(msg)` everywhere, a NullLogger implements the Logger interface but does nothing. Client code calls `logger.log(msg)` unconditionally. Eliminates null checks throughout the codebase.

questions.question: In Python, `None` vs. Null Object: when should you prefer the Null Object?
options: When None checks pollute client code — prefer a do-nothing object implementing the expected protocol
Always use None — it's idiomatic Python
Null Object is only needed in statically typed languages
questions.explanation: Null Object is a design choice, not a language feature. If you call `.execute()` on a possibly-absent strategy 100 times, a NullStrategy is cleaner than 100 `if strategy is not None:` checks. Use contextually.

questions.question: Chain of Responsibility passes a request along:
options: A chain of handlers, each deciding to handle or pass it forward
A chain of commands to undo
questions.explanation: CoR: a pre-trade risk check chain — PositionLimitCheck → MarketRiskCheck → CreditCheck. Each handler processes what it can and passes the rest. Decouples sender from the exact handler(s) that process the request.

questions.question: In C++, lambdas captured in a `std::function` queue implement which pattern combination?
options: Command + Iterator — commands are stored and executed sequentially
questions.explanation: A `std::queue<std::function<void()>>` is a command queue (Command pattern). A loop draining it is an Iterator. This combination is the basis of task queues, event loops, and lock-free work-stealing schedulers.

questions.question: Observer pattern's push vs. pull model: what is the trade-off?
options: Push sends data with notification (lower latency, potential over-delivery); pull lets observers fetch on notification (observers control data, higher latency)
Pull eliminates the need for notifications
questions.explanation: Push: subject sends full data in notification. Pull: subject sends a change event, observer calls back to get data. Push is better for low-latency (fewer round trips). Pull avoids sending irrelevant data to observers.

questions.question: Which behavioral pattern is most appropriate for implementing a trading strategy that changes behavior based on market regime (trending vs. mean-reverting)?
options: State — the strategy object transitions between regime states, changing its algorithm accordingly
Template Method — fixed skeleton with hooks
questions.explanation: State is ideal here: the strategy itself manages its regime state (`TrendingState`, `MeanRevertingState`). When a regime-detection signal fires, the state transitions and algorithm changes transparently to the outer system.

questions.question: Visitor pattern allows:
options: Adding new operations to a class hierarchy without modifying the classes
Adding new classes without modifying operations
questions.explanation: Visitor separates algorithm from object structure. A `RiskCalculatorVisitor` traverses a portfolio hierarchy (Positions, Options, Futures) computing risk without cluttering each class with risk methods. Open/closed principle.

questions.question: In Python, the `__iter__` and `__next__` protocol is the standard implementation of:
questions.explanation: `__iter__` returns the iterator object (often `self`). `__next__` returns the next value or raises `StopIteration`. Every Python for loop uses this. Custom classes implement it to make collections iterable.

questions.question: A FIX order validation pipeline using multiple validators in sequence implements which pattern?
questions.explanation: Each validator (DuplicateOrderCheck, MarginCheck, SymbolCheck) is a handler in a chain. Each runs its check; if it passes, the request moves to the next handler. If it fails, it can reject without continuing.

questions.question: What is the Memento pattern used for?
options: Capturing and externalizing an object's internal state so it can be restored later — for undo functionality
questions.explanation: Memento: `checkpoint = strategy.save_state()` ... `strategy.restore_state(checkpoint)`. Useful for strategy parameter rollback after a bad backtest period, or undo in configuration editors.

questions.question: In C++, which modern feature replaces the classic Strategy interface class?
options: std::function or template policy parameters — both avoid virtual dispatch overhead
Only virtual functions can implement Strategy
questions.explanation: `template<class ExecPolicy> class Engine { ExecPolicy policy; }` — zero-cost compile-time Strategy. Or `std::function<Signal(Bar)>` for runtime strategy. Modern C++ offers both, choose based on performance requirements.

questions.question: Observer pattern vs. event-driven architecture: what is the relationship?
options: Event-driven architectures are a large-scale application of Observer — events are notifications, handlers are observers
Observer requires synchronous notification; EDA is always async
questions.explanation: EDA scales Observer: a message bus (Kafka, Redis) acts as a Subject; microservices subscribe as Observers. The same publish/subscribe semantics, but decoupled via a broker rather than direct reference holding.

questions.question: What is CRTP (Curiously Recurring Template Pattern)?
options: A C++ idiom where a class inherits from a template instantiated with itself: `class Derived : public Base<Derived>`
A runtime polymorphism pattern using virtual functions
A way to implement Singleton with templates
A pattern for managing memory with templates
questions.explanation: CRTP: `template<class T> class Base { void interface() { static_cast<T*>(this)->impl(); } }; class Derived : public Base<Derived> { void impl() {...} };` — static polymorphism with zero virtual dispatch overhead.

questions.question: What advantage does CRTP provide over virtual functions?
options: Zero-overhead static polymorphism — no vtable, no virtual dispatch, compiler can inline everything
CRTP is always easier to read
Virtual functions are not available in modern C++
questions.explanation: Virtual dispatch costs ~1-5ns per call (cache miss on vtable pointer). CRTP resolves at compile time — the call is inlined, zero overhead. Critical in HFT where strategy base classes are called millions of times per second.

questions.question: What is the PIMPL idiom (Pointer to IMPLementation)?
options: Hide implementation details behind a pointer to a forward-declared class, reducing compilation dependencies and binary size
A pattern for implementing multiple interfaces
A smart pointer technique for RAII
A way to implement Singleton with a hidden pointer
questions.explanation: PIMPL: `class Order { struct Impl; std::unique_ptr<Impl> pImpl; };` — Impl is defined only in the .cpp. This breaks header dependencies (no includes needed in header), speeds up compilation, and enables ABI stability.

questions.question: What is the main trade-off of PIMPL?
options: One extra heap allocation and pointer dereference per object — adds latency
questions.explanation: PIMPL costs: 1 heap allocation (mitigated by custom allocator), 1 pointer dereference per access (can cause cache miss). For low-latency code in hot paths, avoid PIMPL. Use it for library APIs and compilation firewalls.

questions.question: Copy-and-swap idiom implements:
options: A strongly exception-safe assignment operator — copy into a temp, then swap with the current object
A pattern for deep copying containers
A way to avoid copy constructors
questions.explanation: `Order& operator=(Order other) { swap(*this, other); return *this; }` — `other` is a copy (handles self-assignment, exception safety). `swap` is noexcept. If the copy throws, `*this` is unchanged. Clean and exception-safe.

questions.question: What does RAII stand for and which pattern does it implement?
options: Resource Acquisition Is Initialization — implements a form of Proxy/Guard that ties resource lifetime to scope
questions.explanation: RAII: acquire in constructor, release in destructor. `std::lock_guard`, `std::unique_ptr`, `std::fstream` all use RAII. It ensures exception-safe resource management — the destructor runs even if an exception is thrown.

questions.question: The LMAX Disruptor is best described as:
options: A lock-free ring buffer with sequenced slots, replacing a queue for inter-thread communication with nanosecond latency
A design pattern for database connections
A networking protocol for low latency
questions.explanation: Disruptor uses a pre-allocated ring buffer, sequence numbers (atomics), and cache-line padding to avoid false sharing. Throughput: 25M+ events/sec. Used in HFT for market data dissemination and order processing pipelines.

questions.question: Why does the LMAX Disruptor pad data to cache line boundaries (typically 64 bytes)?
options: To prevent false sharing — multiple threads modifying adjacent memory in the same cache line causes expensive cache coherency traffic
To improve memory alignment for SIMD
questions.explanation: False sharing: Thread A writes sequence counter, Thread B reads price — if on the same 64-byte cache line, every write by A invalidates B's cache. Padding isolates hot variables to their own cache lines. Critical for Disruptor performance.

questions.question: CRTP is used in the C++ standard library for:
options: std::enable_shared_from_this — base class template that gives derived classes shared_ptr self-referencing ability
questions.explanation: `class MyObj : public std::enable_shared_from_this<MyObj>` uses CRTP. The base template stores a weak_ptr and `shared_from_this()` returns a proper `shared_ptr<MyObj>`. The base needs the derived type to return the right type.

questions.question: What are C++ Mixins in the context of CRTP?
options: Template base classes injecting additional behavior into a derived class without virtual overhead
Runtime mixins added to objects dynamically
Abstract base classes with pure virtual functions
questions.explanation: Mixin via CRTP: `template<class T> struct Serializable { std::string serialize() { return static_cast<T*>(this)->to_string(); } };` — compose behaviors: `class Order : public Serializable<Order>, public Loggable<Order> {}`.

questions.question: In Python, mixins are implemented via:
options: Multiple inheritance with mixin classes listed first — `class Order(SerializableMixin, LoggableMixin, Base)`
questions.explanation: Python MRO (C3 linearization) resolves multiple inheritance. Mixin classes add capabilities without being base classes: `class JSONMixin: def to_json(self): ...` then `class Order(JSONMixin, Base): ...`. Keep mixins small and focused.

questions.question: What is a lock-free Single Producer Single Consumer (SPSC) queue and when is it used in quant systems?
options: A ring buffer where one thread writes and one reads using atomic sequence numbers — no mutex needed, used for market data between IO and strategy threads
questions.explanation: SPSC queue: producer writes to head, consumer reads from tail. No contention — one atomic store/load each. Latency: ~10ns. Common pattern: network thread receives market data, writes to SPSC, strategy thread consumes. Zero lock overhead.

questions.question: Type erasure in C++ (e.g., `std::function`, `std::any`) is related to which pattern?
options: Adapter — it wraps a concrete type behind a uniform interface without virtual inheritance
questions.explanation: Type erasure erases the concrete type behind a stable interface, internally using a vtable-like mechanism. `std::function` wraps any callable behind `operator()`. This is Adapter at the type-system level — runtime polymorphism without inheritance.

questions.question: In Python, `contextlib.contextmanager` implements which C++ idiom?
options: RAII — the `with` statement guarantees cleanup in `__exit__` just as RAII destructor guarantees cleanup on scope exit
questions.explanation: `with open(f) as fh:` guarantees `fh.close()` even on exception — exactly RAII semantics. `__enter__` acquires, `__exit__` releases. Python cannot do destructor-based RAII, so `with` is the idiomatic equivalent.

questions.question: What is 'policy-based design' in C++?
options: Parameterize a class with template policy classes that customize behavior at compile time — zero-overhead Strategy
A runtime design pattern using virtual functions
A way to implement dependency injection
questions.explanation: Policy-based design: `template<class LockPolicy, class AllocPolicy> class OrderBook`. `LockPolicy` can be `Mutex`, `Spinlock`, or `NoLock`. Chosen at compile time — zero overhead vs. runtime strategy. Popularized by Alexandrescu's 'Modern C++ Design'.

questions.question: Why is `std::atomic` preferred over `volatile` for lock-free programming?
options: std::atomic provides memory ordering guarantees (happens-before); volatile only prevents compiler optimization, not CPU reordering
They are equivalent for single variables
questions.explanation: `volatile` tells the compiler not to cache in registers but doesn't prevent CPU out-of-order execution. `std::atomic` with `memory_order_acquire/release` inserts the right memory fences. For lock-free Disruptor sequences, always use `std::atomic<int64_t>`.

questions.question: The Decorator pattern in C++ without virtual functions uses:
questions.explanation: Template Decorator chains at compile time. `LoggingDecorator<T>` wraps T and forwards all calls, adding logging. Zero virtual dispatch. Trade-off: can't swap decorators at runtime, but perfect for known-at-compile-time configurations in HFT.

questions.question: In Python, `__slots__` relates to which optimization pattern?
options: Flyweight — prevents __dict__ creation per instance, reducing memory by storing attributes in a fixed C array
questions.explanation: `__slots__ = ['price', 'qty']` eliminates the per-instance `__dict__`, saving ~200 bytes per object. For 1M tick objects, that's 200MB saved. Flyweight-like optimization: reduce per-instance overhead by removing dynamic attribute storage.

questions.question: What is the expression template technique in C++?
options: Lazy evaluation of expressions using templates — `a + b + c` builds a tree at compile time, evaluated only when assigned — used in linear algebra libraries like Eigen
A way to use templates for string expressions
questions.explanation: Expression templates avoid temporary allocations in `Matrix r = a + b + c`. Instead of 2 temporaries, a compile-time expression tree is built and fused into a single loop. Eigen uses this for zero-overhead vector math — critical for quant risk calculations.

questions.question: Which C++ idiom ensures an object is moved rather than copied when returned from a function?
options: RVO (Return Value Optimization) and NRVO — the compiler elides the copy entirely; std::move for explicit move semantics
questions.explanation: RVO: compiler constructs return value directly in the caller's storage — zero copies. NRVO: same for named variables. `std::move` forces move semantics when RVO can't apply. Modern C++ move semantics eliminates most expensive copies.

questions.question: In HFT, why is branch prediction important and which pattern minimizes unpredictable branches?
options: CPU mispredictions cost ~15 cycles; State pattern with virtual dispatch has predictable indirect branches; strategy tables (function pointer arrays) avoid if-else chains
Branch prediction only matters for sorting algorithms
questions.explanation: CPU branch predictor trains on history. A strategy-dispatch table (`handlers[msg_type](msg)`) is a predictable indirect branch — one lookup. A chain of `if (type == X)` with random inputs causes mispredictions. Choose data-oriented dispatch in hot paths.

questions.question: What is the Curiously Recurring Template Pattern used for in C++ linear algebra libraries?
options: Static interface enforcement — `Base<Derived>` can call `Derived`-specific methods without virtual dispatch, used in Eigen for expression templates
questions.explanation: Eigen uses CRTP extensively: `MatrixBase<Derived>` provides operations like `.transpose()`, `.norm()` that delegate to `Derived`'s actual storage. No virtual calls — the compiler knows all types at compile time and can fully optimize.

questions.question: Python's `abc.ABC` and `@abstractmethod` provide which C++ equivalent?
options: Pure virtual functions (`virtual void method() = 0`) — forces subclasses to implement the method or remain abstract
questions.explanation: `@abstractmethod` in Python ≈ `= 0` in C++. Both prevent instantiation of the base class and force derived classes to implement the method. Python enforces this at instantiation time; C++ at compile time.

questions.question: When should you prefer compile-time (template) polymorphism over runtime (virtual) polymorphism in C++?
options: When the type set is known at compile time and performance is critical — templates eliminate vtable overhead; use virtual when you need runtime extensibility
Always use templates — they are always faster
Virtual functions are always preferred for clarity
questions.explanation: Rule of thumb: if all types are known when you compile (HFT strategy, math library), use templates for zero overhead. If types are determined at runtime (plugin systems, serialization), use virtual. Know the cost: ~1-5ns virtual dispatch vs. 0ns inlined template call.

questions.question: The LMAX Disruptor's ring buffer size must be a power of two. Why?
options: So index wrapping uses bitwise AND (`index & (size-1)`) instead of modulo — bitwise AND is 1 cycle vs. modulo which can be 20-40 cycles
questions.explanation: `index % 1024` costs a division (20-40 cycles on modern CPUs). `index & 1023` is a single bitwise AND (1 cycle). In a Disruptor processing 25M events/sec, this optimization matters. Power-of-2 ring buffers are a universal low-latency pattern.

questions.question: What does std::thread do when its destructor runs while the thread is still joinable?
questions.explanation: If a joinable thread is destroyed without join() or detach(), std::terminate() is called. Always RAII-wrap threads.

questions.question: Which RAII wrapper in C++20 automatically joins a thread on destruction?
questions.explanation: std::jthread (C++20) calls join() in its destructor and also supports stop tokens for cooperative cancellation.

questions.question: What is the result of calling std::thread::hardware_concurrency()?
options: A hint for the number of hardware threads (may return 0)
The number of available CPU cores, always accurate
questions.explanation: hardware_concurrency() is a hint and may return 0 if the value is not computable. Do not treat it as exact.

questions.question: After std::thread::detach() is called, which statement is true?
options: You can still call join() on it
questions.explanation: After detach(), the thread runs independently and the std::thread object becomes non-joinable (joinable() returns false).

questions.question: What is a data race in C++?
options: Two threads reading the same variable
Two threads accessing the same memory where at least one is a write, with no synchronization
A race to acquire the same mutex
questions.explanation: A data race is undefined behavior: two concurrent accesses to the same location, at least one write, with no happens-before relationship.

questions.question: Which pattern avoids the 'thread not joined before destructor' problem?
questions.explanation: A thread_guard RAII class stores a reference to the thread and calls join() in its destructor, ensuring cleanup even on exception.

questions.question: When passing arguments to std::thread, how do you pass by reference?
options: Pass directly -- std::thread always passes by reference
questions.explanation: std::thread copies arguments by default. Use std::ref() to pass by reference, and be careful about lifetime -- the referenced variable must outlive the thread.

questions.question: What is std::this_thread::yield() used for?
options: Hints to the scheduler to reschedule -- lets other threads run
questions.explanation: yield() is a hint to the scheduler that the current thread is willing to give up its time slice, allowing other runnable threads to execute.

questions.question: What does thread_local storage guarantee?
options: Each thread has its own copy of the variable
The variable is shared between threads safely
The variable is zero-initialized only on the main thread
questions.explanation: thread_local gives each thread its own independent copy of the variable, initialized on first use in that thread. No synchronization needed.

questions.question: In the context of C++ threads, what does 'ownership' refer to?
options: Which std::thread object is responsible for the underlying thread
Which thread holds the highest priority
The thread that allocated the most memory
questions.explanation: Thread ownership means which std::thread object owns the OS thread. Ownership is movable (via move semantics) but not copyable.

questions.question: Which std::thread operation is NOT possible?
options: Moving a thread to another std::thread object
questions.explanation: std::thread is move-only. Copying is deleted because it would be ambiguous about which object owns the thread.

questions.question: What does std::thread::get_id() return for a default-constructed (non-running) thread?
questions.explanation: A default-constructed thread has id == std::thread::id{}, which is distinct from any running thread's ID.

questions.question: What happens if you call join() on a thread that has already been joined?
questions.explanation: Calling join() on a non-joinable thread (already joined, detached, or default-constructed) throws std::system_error.

questions.question: In the producer-consumer pattern with threads, what ensures the consumer does not busy-spin?
questions.explanation: condition_variable::wait() atomically releases the mutex and blocks the thread until notified, avoiding busy-spinning.

questions.question: Which is a correct way to launch a thread that runs a member function?
questions.explanation: Use pointer-to-member: std::thread(&Class::method, &obj, args...). A lambda capturing the object by reference also works.

questions.question: What is the purpose of std::call_once with std::once_flag?
options: Ensure a function is called exactly once across all threads, safely
Call a function once per thread
Guard a critical section with a mutex
questions.explanation: std::call_once guarantees that a callable is executed exactly once even when called concurrently from multiple threads. Ideal for lazy initialization.

questions.question: Which C++ idiom provides thread-safe lazy singleton initialization with zero explicit synchronization?
options: Static local variable (guaranteed thread-safe since C++11)
questions.explanation: Since C++11, static local variable initialization is guaranteed thread-safe (Magic Statics). The compiler emits the necessary synchronization.

questions.question: What is the 'happens-before' relationship?
options: A guarantee that all effects of operation A are visible to operation B
The order in which threads are created
questions.explanation: Happens-before is the formal C++ memory model concept: if A happens-before B, all memory writes by A are visible to B. Synchronization operations establish this.

questions.question: What does std::this_thread::sleep_for(100ms) guarantee?
options: The thread sleeps AT LEAST 100ms (may sleep longer)
The thread yields for 100 CPU cycles
The thread suspends until another thread notifies it
questions.explanation: sleep_for sleeps for at least the given duration. OS scheduling and clock resolution mean the actual sleep is often slightly longer.

questions.question: In a thread pool, what data structure is typically used to pass work items?
questions.explanation: Thread pools use a thread-safe work queue -- typically a std::queue protected by a mutex + condition_variable, or a lock-free queue for performance.

questions.question: What is the difference between parallelism and concurrency?
options: Concurrency is about structure (dealing with many tasks); parallelism is about execution (doing many things simultaneously)
Parallelism requires multiple cores; concurrency does not
Concurrency is always faster than parallelism
questions.explanation: Concurrency is a design property: structuring a program to handle multiple tasks. Parallelism is a runtime property: actually executing tasks simultaneously on multiple cores.

questions.question: What is a race condition (distinct from a data race)?
options: A bug where program correctness depends on the relative timing of events
An atomic operation failing under contention
std::terminate being called from a thread
questions.explanation: A race condition is a higher-level bug where the outcome depends on thread interleaving. Data races are a specific type involving unsynchronized memory access.

questions.question: Why is 'volatile' NOT a substitute for proper thread synchronization in C++?
options: volatile only prevents compiler caching but provides no memory ordering guarantees between threads
volatile variables cannot be passed to threads
questions.explanation: volatile prevents the compiler from caching a variable in a register, but provides no cross-thread visibility guarantees. Use std::atomic or mutex for thread safety.

questions.question: What is std::thread::id?
options: A hash of the thread's stack pointer
An opaque type that uniquely identifies a running thread
The index of the thread in a thread pool
questions.explanation: std::thread::id is an opaque, comparable type that uniquely identifies a thread. Useful for logging, debugging, and detecting recursive lock attempts.

questions.question: What is the 'spurious wakeup' problem with condition variables?
options: A condition variable that wakes up a thread not waiting on it
A thread waking from wait() even though notify was not called -- always recheck the predicate
A deadlock caused by two condition variables
A condition variable that is never signaled
questions.explanation: Spurious wakeups are wakeups without a corresponding notify. Always use the predicate form: cv.wait(lock, [&]{ return condition; }); to recheck.

questions.question: What is the difference between std::mutex::lock() and std::mutex::try_lock()?
options: lock() blocks until acquired; try_lock() returns immediately with false if unavailable
lock() supports recursive locking; try_lock() does not
questions.explanation: lock() blocks the calling thread until the mutex is acquired. try_lock() attempts acquisition and returns false immediately if it fails.

questions.question: Why should you prefer std::lock_guard over manual lock()/unlock() calls?
options: lock_guard is RAII: it unlocks the mutex in its destructor even if an exception is thrown
questions.explanation: RAII ensures the mutex is always released when lock_guard goes out of scope, preventing deadlocks from missed unlock() calls or exceptions.

questions.question: What is std::unique_lock's advantage over std::lock_guard?
options: It allows deferred locking, manual unlock/lock, and can be moved -- needed for condition variables
It works with recursive mutexes automatically
questions.explanation: unique_lock is more flexible: you can defer locking, unlock early, and move ownership. Condition variable wait() requires unique_lock.

questions.question: What is the classic deadlock scenario with two mutexes?
options: Thread A locks M1 then M2; Thread B locks M2 then M1 -- circular wait
Thread A calls try_lock() and fails
Two threads locking the same mutex
A thread calling lock() twice on the same mutex
questions.explanation: Circular wait: A holds M1, waits for M2; B holds M2, waits for M1. Neither can proceed. Prevention: always acquire locks in a consistent order.

questions.question: How does std::lock() (free function) prevent deadlock when locking multiple mutexes?
options: It locks them in alphabetical order
It uses a deadlock-free algorithm (try-and-back-off) to acquire all locks atomically
It creates a temporary mutex ordering
questions.explanation: std::lock(m1, m2) uses a deadlock-free algorithm. Order does not matter. Follow with lock_guard(m, std::adopt_lock).

questions.question: What does std::scoped_lock (C++17) do?
